en: The guiding hypothesis, confirmed in the end, was that the difficulty did not lie in an absence of normative basis, but in the persistence of an ontologically impoverished reading of the CDC itself.<1>p. 793-794</1>

The Brazilian legal order is already open enough to accommodate the protection of these goods, provided that art. 3, §1, is reread with a dogmatic density compatible with the contemporary informational economy. What was missing was not a new legislative microsystem for the digital, but a conceptual reconstruction capable of lifting the immaterial good out of the residual position in which it had been kept and bringing it back to the center of the protective regime.<1>p. 794</1>

The central shift is from a static ontology of the good to a functional ontology of enjoyment, and the jurist comes to ask under what conditions the object remains usable, intelligible, recognizable and substantially equivalent to what justified the acquisition. On that basis, the regime is articulated in a single sentence. Qualification comes through the IOC, asymmetry through semiotic vulnerability, governed expectation through hypercuratorial anticipation, the unlawful act through abusive teleology, control of changes through open auditability and functional value equivalence, containment of exclusivity through the social function, and remedies through functional restoration and regime correction. The two control criteria have a disciplining function, because they prevent the critique of opacity and mutability from degenerating into rhetoric or nostalgia.

Without open auditability, the critique of opacity risks becoming rhetoric without a knowable object. Without functional value equivalence, the critique of mutability risks becoming naive nostalgia for an impossible stability.<1>p. 795</1>

Thus, the axis of analysis shifts from a static ontology of the good to a functional ontology of enjoyment. Instead of asking only what the object is in the abstract, it is now possible to ask under what conditions it remains usable, intelligible, recognizable and substantially equivalent to what justified the acquisition and sustained the consumer's legitimate expectation.<1>p. 794</1>

The regime sets out to coherently articulate the qualification of the immaterial product by the Immaterial Object of Consumption, the location of the relevant asymmetry by semiotic vulnerability, the reading of governed expectation by hypercuratorial anticipation, the identification of the unlawful act by abusive teleology, the control of changes by open auditability and functional value equivalence, the containment of exclusivity by the social function of property and of intellectual property, and the reorganization of remedies around functional restoration and regime correction.<1>p. 800</1>

The practical gain lies in translation. The justice system often senses that losses of accounts, digital goods, history and position in the environment exceed the immediate patrimonial dimension, but it lacks a stable grammar to ground that perception, and it oscillates between downgrading the conflict to contractual annoyance and perceiving it as serious without being able to say what was injured. The categories of the regime reduce this translation cost, because they bring conflicts back inside the CDC without inflating the system or exchanging it for theories external to positive law.

The justice system often senses that losses relating to accounts, digital goods, usage history and position in the environment exceed the immediate patrimonial dimension, but it lacks a sufficiently stable dogmatic grammar to turn that perception into rigorous grounding. Hence the oscillation between two equally unsatisfactory reductions. Either the conflict is downgraded to a low-density contractual annoyance, or it is perceived as intuitively serious without anyone being able to say precisely, in controllable legal language, what exactly was injured and why.<1>p. 800</1>

One of the most relevant gains of this thesis lies in reducing this translation cost, providing categories able to bring these conflicts back inside the CDC without inflating the system or abandoning it in favor of theories external to positive law.<1>p. 800</1>

The ethics that sustains all this is one of containment, not demolition. The goal is neither to abolish platforms nor to romanticize a world without technology. This ethics is condensed in the Egyptian myth of Isis and Ra, in which the goddess does not want to annihilate the sun but to make it reveal the name it keeps to itself, because power once named stops operating as a pure natural presence and becomes invocable, delimitable and bound to answer. What Consumer Law lacks before the law of the platform is not moral indignation but the vocabulary to make demonstrable the decisions that today pass for the mere functioning of the system.
Law is not asked to put out the sun. It is asked to make it say its name.<1>p. 793</1>
The goal is not to abolish platforms, nor to romanticize a world without technology, something intellectually limiting and institutionally useless.<1>p. 793</1>
What questions remain open?

The scope has limits. This is not a total theory of platforms or of digital consumption, illustrative examples do not replace broad empirical research, and the institutional operationalization of the criteria is far from exhausted, because open auditability and functional value equivalence will still require evidentiary maturation, refinement in expert evidence and decision protocols more sensitive to the opacity of platform conflicts.

At the same time, there is no intention to offer a total theory of digital consumption, nor to exhaustively map the plurality of platform ecosystems that today organize work, cultural circulation, sociability, economic intermediation and everyday experience.<1>p. 801</1>

Nor is there any intention to replace broad empirical research with illustrative exemplification, or to exhaust the institutional operationalization of the proposed standards. Open auditability and functional value equivalence will require, in the future, evidentiary maturation, expert refinement and the development of decision protocols more sensitive to the structural opacity of platform conflicts.<1>p. 801</1>

The first open question is the limit hypothesis of the platform that fails. The problem lies not only in the opportunistic platform that alters rules or degrades functions while it operates, but also in the one whose technical or economic failure may produce an even more radical loss. That loss is the possible erasure of the digital world as an infrastructure of enjoyment, when the biographical continuity, patrimonial memory and sociability of thousands or millions of consumers depend on servers, accounts, libraries, databases and execution environments. For the shutdown of the service, the constitutional order already requires reconciling it, as far as technically and legally possible, with continuity, portability, functional restoration or assignment of the operation. For failure, the question is posed whether the Law can go on treating business closure as a simple exercise of economic freedom when it results in the burial of collections, identities, reputations and histories.
In continuous consumer relations, no intellectual property right justifies, on its own, the complete extinction of the infrastructure with the consequent complete sacrifice of the IOCs.<1>p. 796</1>

The limit hypothesis, at this point, is not only the opportunistic platform that alters rules, degrades functionalities or intensifies value extraction while it remains operational. It is also the platform that fails.<1>p. 796</1>

When the functional value equivalence, biographical continuity, patrimonial memory and accumulated sociability of thousands or millions of consumers depend on the permanence of servers, accounts, libraries, databases, authentication systems and execution environments, the technical or economic failure of the supplier may produce an even more radical form of loss. It is not merely an abusive alteration of the digital world, but its possible erasure as an infrastructure of enjoyment.<1>p. 796-797</1>

If the shutdown of the service is unavoidable, the constitutional order requires that it be reconciled, as far as technically and legally possible, with solutions of continuity, portability, functional restoration, assignment of the operation or other measures suitable to prevent private architecture from becoming a lawful instrument of patrimonial and existential devastation of the consumer.<1>p. 796</1>

The question that emerges is whether the Law can go on treating business closure as a simple exercise of economic freedom when it results in the burial of collections, identities, reputations, histories and immaterial objects of consumption incorporated into the practical life of consumers.<1>p. 797</1>

The second is the concern about behavioral decipherment, which has not yet received the centrality its gravity would deserve. In these ecosystems, the platform not only governs the enjoyment of the acquired object, but may progressively learn to decipher the subject who enjoys it. It then comes to know that subject as pattern, predictability and susceptibility, which shifts the asymmetry to a plane in which the supplier may hold means of psycho-functional reconstruction of the user that the user does not have over themselves. The problem remains a hypothesis, reveals a deeper reach of semiotic vulnerability and calls for future development, with consequences still little examined for autonomy, practical freedom and the integrity of personality.

There is, however, an additional consequence of this model that, although it was not explored throughout the development with the centrality its gravity would deserve, imposes itself at least as an unavoidable theoretical concern at the end of the crossing. In continuous digital ecosystems, especially in sectoral models analogous to the one studied, the platform not only governs the enjoyment of the acquired object, but may progressively learn to decipher the very subject who enjoys it.<1>p. 798</1>

The point deserves special care because, in this scenario, the platform no longer knows the consumer only as an account holder, acquirer of content or recipient of targeted advertising. It comes to know them as a pattern. As predictability. As susceptibility.<1>p. 798-799</1>

The asymmetry, then, is no longer limited to the informational plane in the ordinary sense, nor is it exhausted in the supplier's technical superiority regarding the internal functioning of the system. It shifts to a more delicate plane, in which the supplier comes to hold means of psycho-functional reconstruction of the user that the user does not possess over themselves with an equivalent degree of operative precision.<1>p. 799</1>
Semiotic vulnerability, from this perspective, reveals an even deeper reach than initially formulated.<1>p. 799</1>

The challenge facing Consumer Law, therefore, is not only to limit abusive mutations of enjoyment, but to confront, in future development, the possibility that continuous platform consumption becomes a private technique for producing intensive subjective legibility, with consequences still insufficiently examined for autonomy, for practical freedom and for the very integrity of personality in digitally governed environments.<1>p. 800</1>

Therein lies the reason for the remedies. What presents itself as the simple functioning of the system can be reconstructed as choice, as program and, when necessary, as abuse, and only then does it become possible to restore degraded enjoyment, contest opaque decisions and rebuild trust.

The Brazilian constitutional order does not require the elimination of the private infrastructures that organize contemporary experience; it requires, rather, that the power inscribed in them let itself be seen, proven, limited and, when necessary, corrected.<1>p. 802</1>
What presents itself as the simple functioning of the system can and must be reconstructed as choice, as program and, when necessary, as abuse.<1>p. 801</1>

Only then will it be possible to restore degraded enjoyment, contest opaque decisions and rebuild trust without accepting that power organized by architecture should present itself as a mere, inevitable backdrop.<1>p. 793</1>

Why technique changes the legal question
Why is saying it was just an update not enough to close the case?

The conflict this chapter prepares begins with a familiar answer. The consumer buys an item, a subscription or access, what it offers later changes, and the supplier explains that there was a system change, a normal update or an unavoidable service event. These expressions only sound like an answer as long as consumption is read through a strictly material ontology, and that is why the background against which the relationship unfolds is described first, before formulating the categories capable of making these losses attributable and controllable. Against that background, the experience takes the form of permanence in a governed environment, where the interface organizes access, induces choices, limits alternatives and distributes rewards or sanctions.
Contemporary digital consumption can no longer be adequately understood as the simple acquisition of a thing or the contracting of a one-off service.<1>p. 83</1>

When technique operates as environment and the platform operates as market architecture, the consumer relationship comes to be traversed by regimes of access, data, interface and technical and legal exclusivities that condition delivery, enjoyment and the effective space of choice. It is this background that sustains the formulation of categories able to render attributable and controllable those losses and asymmetries that, under a strictly material ontology of consumption, would tend to appear as “system change”, “normal update” or “unavoidable service event”.<1>p. 85</1>

In many ecosystems, the experience takes the form of permanence in a governed environment, in which the interface organizes access, induces choices, limits alternatives and distributes rewards or sanctions.<1>p. 83</1>

The platform, in this picture, does not merely put buyers and sellers in contact. It organizes markets, administers access, structures dependencies and converts circulation into continuous value extraction, and infrastructure, data, interface and operating rules come to compose a single arrangement, in which performance is prolonged and the bond is renewed through frictions and incentives. Economic rationality, therefore, materializes in design, curation and execution protocols, and the practical normativity of the environment does not derive only from texts, contracts or explicit commands. The decisive turn occurs when mediation ceases to be perceived as a neutral channel and comes to operate as a form of organizing experience, so that technique and media frame the possible, define the relevant and stabilize certain conducts as normal through repetition, convenience and design.

Infrastructure, data, interface and operating rules come to compose a single arrangement, in which performance is prolonged, the bond is renewed through frictions and incentives, and the capture of attention and diffuse productivity is part of the ordinary functioning of the service.<1>p. 83</1>

In this regime, technique and media constitute practical ambiences: they frame the possible, define the relevant and stabilize certain conducts as normal through repetition, convenience and design.<1>p. 83</1>

This creates a precise difficulty for the jurist. In continuous digital services, the supplier usually treats the modulation of what can be enjoyed as an ordinary operation of the system, while the consumer forms expectations of enjoyment and belonging from what was promised, acquired and experienced. This distance produces qualificatory opacity, which makes it hard to name the injury, identify the affected object and bring the loss back to the traditional categories of adequacy, quality, defect and information. The answer is to treat architecture and governance as a material dimension of supply, and not as a setting external to it, because the enjoyment of the object becomes inseparable from the functioning of the technical ambience.

This distance between regimes of meaning produces qualificatory opacity: it makes it hard to name the injury, identify the affected object and bring the loss back to the traditional categories of adequacy, quality, defect and information. Therefore, architecture and governance must be treated as a material dimension of supply.<1>p. 88-89</1>

The enjoyment of the object becomes inseparable from the functioning of the technical ambience, which is why architecture and governance cannot be treated as externalities of supply, but as material dimensions of the consumer relationship itself.<1>p. 98</1>

It is at this point that the defense that the change is just how software works loses force. It presents as a property of technique what results from socially situated choices, shaped by interests, disputes and purposes, and that only seems inevitable because it has come to operate as a naturalized environment. This mechanism of naturalization hides purposes, hinders contestation and moves the conflict outside the ordinary sphere of accountability. If technical architecture organizes the consumer experience, it cannot be treated as nature and must be read as design, and design is open to critique, control and reorientation.

If technical architecture becomes a vector for organizing everyday life, it also becomes a locus of attribution and of assessment of legitimacy, above all when it begins to structure choices, expectations and regimes of access that cannot be audited by their addressees or even by legitimate authorities.<1>p. 88</1>

The systemic force of technique does not eliminate the fact that artifacts, infrastructures and platforms take concrete forms through socially situated choices, shaped by interests, disputes and purposes. This passage is decisive for the thesis: if technical architecture organizes the consumer experience, it cannot be treated as nature. It must be read as design, and design is open to critique, control and reorientation.<1>p. 88</1>

In the context of this research, this means that the appearance of inevitability of platforms must also be read as the result of consolidated choices, which come to operate as a naturalized environment. It is this mechanism of naturalization that makes the architecture of platforms legally relevant: it hides purposes, hinders contestation and moves conflicts outside the ordinary sphere of accountability.<1>p. 88</1>
Why does Consumer Law draw on authors from outside law?

This background is organized in three conceptual sets, each with its own function, precisely so that it is not reduced to a sociological impression. The first, which this chapter covers, reconstructs the passage of technique and media from tools to environments of life, with Jacques Ellul, Neil Postman and Willem H. Vanderburg in the diagnosis and Andrew Feenberg in the critical key that rules out determinism and preserves the controllability of technical choices. The second reconstructs the political economy of platforms as an arrangement of extraction, toll and dependence, with Yanis Varoufakis and Ladislau Dowbor, in dialogue with categories of Karl Marx. The third bridges political economy and the semiotics of consumption through the anthropology of Mary Douglas, Baron Isherwood, Arjun Appadurai, Igor Kopytoff and Grant McCracken, and the last two are left for other chapters.

To describe this background without turning it into a mere sociological impression, three conceptual sets are mobilized, each with its own function. The first reconstructs the passage of technique and media from tools to environments of life, in which efficiency, automatism and integration act as criteria of social organization, without eliminating the institutional dispute over design and governance. On this axis, Jacques Ellul, Neil Postman and Willem H. Vanderburg provide the diagnosis of the technical-media ambience, while Andrew Feenberg introduces the critical key needed to rule out determinism and preserve the controllability of technical choices.<1>p. 83-84</1>

The second set reconstructs the political economy of platforms as an arrangement of extraction, toll and dependence, in which digital infrastructures function as private territories of market administration, supply coordination and capture of distributed value. Yanis Varoufakis and Ladislau Dowbor offer the main lenses of this reconstruction, in dialogue with the critique of political economy and with categories of Karl Marx mobilized to clarify the technical and economic form of extraction in digital environments.<1>p. 84</1>

The third set operates as a bridge between political economy and the semiotics of consumption, describing how value, belonging and recognition become organizing components of experience and practical conditions for stabilizing extraction. At this point, the anthropology of consumption, drawn from Mary Douglas, Baron Isherwood, Arjun Appadurai, Igor Kopytoff and Grant McCraken, allows us to understand that consumed objects do not circulate only by utility or price, but through regimes of meaning that sustain bond, distinction and permanence.<1>p. 84-85</1>

How these authors are used matters as much as the choice of them. The references from political economy, sociology, philosophy, anthropology of consumption and communication theory come in to guide the identification of mechanisms and discipline inferences, without exegetical reconstruction of the works. When a concept is taken as a tool to read an object different from the one in which it was born, what matters is what it makes visible in the observed field and how much it improves the legal intelligibility of the problem, and the full genealogy only comes in when it is indispensable to avoid distortion. The theoretical reconstruction is therefore organized by problems and not by an inventory of authors, and each of them appears in this chapter for what it changes in the question the jurist puts to the case.

The theoretical reconstruction that precedes the dogmatic stage is organized by functional axes and by problems, and not by an exegetical inventory of authors. The object analyzed is contemporary, dynamic and institutionally hybrid, so that intelligibility depends less on “explaining authors” than on describing mechanisms that operate in the service and then bringing them back to legal parameters of protection.<1>p. 49</1>

Within the first set, each author fulfills a different function. Ellul allows us to understand the tendency of technical rationality to become autonomous, oriented by efficiency, predictability and control. Postman shifts the problem to media as a form of life, which alters the criteria of relevance, intelligibility and truth. Vanderburg adds the critique of desymbolization, that is, of the reorganization of signs, needs and cultural bonds by advertising and by the technical rationality of consumption. What changes when technique stops being a tool and becomes an environment?

Ellul describes modern technique as a system of rationalization that ceases to be an instrument subordinate to external ends and comes to condition practices, expectations and institutions. For the jurist, what counts is the effect of this rationality on the form of the debate. In whatever domain it is applied, technique presents itself as a rational process and turns the social problem into a problem of method, so that alternatives come to be filtered by what can be rationalized, measured and operationalized. When the automatism of technical choice sets in, the question of what should be preserved gives way to the question of what best keeps the system running.

The Ellulian notion of the autonomization of technique allows us to understand how efficiency comes to operate as the dominant criterion of social organization. Technique ceases to figure as a simple instrument subordinate to external purposes and comes to constitute a system of rationalization capable of conditioning practices, expectations and institutions.<1>p. 92</1>

Ellul <1>(1968)</1> insists that the technical phenomenon cannot be treated as a particular sector of modernity, because it tends to traverse the very elements of civilization. The decisive point is that, in whatever domain it is applied, technique presents itself as a rational process, which shifts the social problem into a problem of method <2>Ellul</2><3>(Ellul, 1968, p. 81)</3>. Alternatives come to be filtered by what can be rationalized, measured and operationalized, and the debate about ends tends to be compressed by the grammar of efficiency.<4>p. 86-87</4>

It is in this context that Ellul describes the automatism of technical choice as a blind search for the “best way” to perform a task, with the loss of a holistic criterion of adequacy and growing indifference to the social, moral or aesthetic consequences produced by the method <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 82-88)</2>. When this automatism sets in, the question of what should be preserved gives way to the question of what best keeps the system running.<3>p. 93</3>

This key appears, on a reduced scale, in platform-operated games. The unilateral alteration of a cosmetic item, which changes the character's appearance, or the redesign of a character do not arise as extraordinary events, but as ordinary manifestations of a system that adjusts itself according to internal criteria of efficiency, balance and retention. Ellul serves to explain why this logic tends to shift the debate from the field of ends, of what should be preserved and of the expectations that were produced, to the field of method, of what works best for the system. It is in this shift that technical design reveals itself as a site of power and as a relevant dimension for legal qualification.

Ellul is mobilized to explain why this logic tends to shift the debate from the field of ends, that is, of what should be preserved and of the expectations that were produced, to the field of method, that is, of what “works best” for the system. With this, technical design reveals itself as a locus of power and as a relevant dimension for subsequent legal qualification.<1>p. 92</1>

The clearest example is League of Legends matchmaking, the system that assembles matches. The company describes the need to balance fair matches, position preference and fast queues at the same time, and admits that, in the face of real constraints, the system redistributes weight among these criteria and relaxes parameters so that the match can happen. Fairness ceases to operate as moral language and comes to function as a statistical target, that of an approximate 50% probability of victory per team, calculated from the MMR average. The company declares this number secret and created to work with back-end systems, the layer that operates on the platform's servers, outside the user's view and control. What happens here is a shift of the relevant decision procedure to a non-transparent layer, and a technical choice presented as inevitable because it works best for the system.

Technical autonomy, here, lies in the shift of the relevant decision procedure to a non-transparent layer, responsible for defining what counts as balance and for continuously adjusting matchmaking criteria to preserve the stability of the ecosystem.<1>p. 94</1>

The result corresponds to the effect described by Ellul: a technical choice presented as inevitable because it “works best” for the system, shifting the debate from ends to the continuous adjustment of method.<1>p. 94</1>

The same normalization appears in the contractual frame. Under the Terms of Service, the user agrees that the company may alter, modify, update, suspend, apply a nerf, which is the deliberate reduction of the power of a game element, or restrict access to features and parts of the service, including through automatic background updates, with or without prior notice. The vocabulary that legitimizes this plasticity is that of constant improvement, evolution and security, and the user's experience comes to be treated as an adjustable dimension of the functioning of the system. Read with Ellul, the clause shows technique affirmed as an environment that justifies itself and absorbs enjoyment as a management variable.

In an Ellulian key, technique ceases to appear as a means subordinate to the purpose of entertainment and affirms itself as a self-justified environment, capable of absorbing enjoyment as a management variable to preserve the stability of the ecosystem.<1>p. 94-95</1>

Ellul extends the diagnosis to law itself. Law is affected not only because it comes to deal with technically complex objects, but because its practice can be absorbed by criteria of efficiency. For what Ellul calls the technician of law, the decisive reference tends to stop being the normative purpose and to become the efficiency of application, and normative conflicts tend to be recast as problems of management and compliance. Since what cannot be rationalized tends to be treated as irrelevant or external to the functioning of the system, technical choices need to be put back in the field of attribution, because the appearance of neutrality may conceal purposes, costs and distributions of risk that directly affect the consumer experience.

The Law is affected by this pressure not only because it comes to deal with technically complex objects, but because its own practice can be absorbed by criteria of efficiency. For the “technician of law”, the decisive reference tends to stop being the normative purpose and becomes the efficiency of application, since “all law depends on its efficiency” and “a law that is not applied is not a law” <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 299)</2>. Under this pressure for performance and operability, normative conflicts tend to be reconfigured as problems of management and compliance, making it harder to deliberate about ends when technical autonomy narrows the space of choice over collective means and directions <3>Ellul</3><4>(Ellul, 1968, p. 143)</4>.<5>p. 97</5>

What cannot be rationalized tends to be treated as irrelevant, impracticable or external to the functioning of the system. Hence the importance of putting technical choices back in the field of attribution, since the appearance of neutrality may conceal purposes, costs and distributions of risk that directly affect the consumer experience.<1>p. 96</1>

Transposed to digital consumption, the diagnosis allows us to read electronic games, streaming platforms and social networks as manifestations of a technique that functions as environment, in which interfaces, algorithms, reward systems and mechanisms of artificial scarcity are organized by criteria of efficiency, retention and continuous governance. It is from this operation that the category of the Immaterial Object of Consumption emerges, an object of functional and continued existence, inseparable from the technical infrastructure that gives it access, utility, stability and practical meaning. Hence the insufficiency of a strictly material reading of consumption, because the central problem is no longer only the existence of a defect in an isolated product and comes to include the way technique organizes the possibilities of use, permanence, loss or degradation over time.

Transposed to digital consumption, this diagnosis allows us to interpret electronic games, streaming platforms and social networks not as isolated applications, but as specific manifestations of this technique-environment.
