What is prepared here under the category of the Immaterial Object of Consumption emerges precisely from this operation: it is an object of functional and continued existence, inseparable from the technical infrastructure that confers on it access, utility, stability and practical meaning. Therefore, a strictly material reading of consumption does not adequately capture the phenomenon. When the object is inseparable from the technical architecture that sustains it, the central problem is no longer only the existence of a defect in an isolated product and comes to include the way technique organizes possibilities of use, permanence, loss or degradation over time.<1>p. 97</1>
How does the consumer come to know what they bought?

Postman, in Amusing Ourselves to Death, allows us to treat media as a form of organizing social knowledge, and not as a simple channel of messages. He matters not for television as a historical object, but for the mechanism, the finding that the form of the medium alters the form of socially practicable rationality. On platforms, the mechanism intensifies through three shifts in the ecology of attention, from uniform diffusion to personalized distribution, from passive reception to continuous interaction and from crude audience metrics to fine metrification of conduct.
Postman <1>(2006)</1> allows us to understand media as a form of organizing social knowledge, and not only as a channel for the circulation of messages.<2>p. 98</2>
The central point is not television as an isolated historical object, but the finding that the form of the medium alters the form of socially practicable rationality.<1>p. 103</1>

In transposing Postman's diagnosis to the digital environment, the decisive point is not to assert that television became the internet, but to identify structural shifts in the ecology of attention: from uniform diffusion to personalized distribution; from predominantly passive reception to continuous interaction; from crude audience metrics to fine metrification of conduct.<1>p. 103</1>

For consumption, the consequence is that the decision ceases to depend mainly on checks of adequacy and performance and comes to be mediated by regimes of attention, reputation and belonging, in which storefronts, trailers, events and narratives of permanent updating are part of the consumed experience itself. In the platform-operated game, official media does not merely publicize what already exists, because it defines what counts as relevant information about the object, which traits should be perceived as essential and which affects serve as criteria of evaluation. The consumer recognizes the item as a desirable good without knowing it as a technical structure. A music video such as POP/STARS, from Riot's music division, turns a set of cosmetics into a public cultural reference prior to use, and the season cinematic Still Here, with the statement Fight for tomorrow, guides the community's gaze and expectation. The knowledge the consumer forms about the item is not expanded access to data, but mediated knowledge in which the image becomes a criterion of pragmatic truth.
The item is what the media allows it to be seen as being.<1>p. 100</1>

The consumption decision ceases to depend primarily on checks of adequacy and performance and comes to be mediated by regimes of attention, reputation and belonging. In them, the form of presentation and the dramaturgy of the offer, expressed in storefronts, trailers, events and narratives of permanent updating, become a constitutive component of the consumed experience.<1>p. 99</1>

Media does not merely publicize what already exists, since it is capable of defining what counts as relevant information about the object, which traits should be perceived as essential and which affects can operate as criteria of evaluation. The consumer does not need to know the item as a technical structure to recognize it as a desirable good.<1>p. 99</1>

A music video such as POP/STARS <1>fonte</1><2>(K/DA..., 2018)</2>, an example of the productivity of the Riot Music division, is especially relevant because it turns a set of cosmetics into a public cultural reference prior to use, operating as a matrix of intelligibility for the purchase and for the social recognition of the item's value.<3>p. 99</3>

Still Here <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024d)</2>, by presenting itself as a season-opening cinematic and condensing the editorial statement “Fight for tomorrow”, makes explicit this function of guiding gaze and expectation. The epistemology of consumption, here, does not correspond to expanded access to data about the object, but to a form of mediated knowledge in which the image becomes a criterion of pragmatic truth.<3>p. 99-100</3>

The contract, however, describes the same object in another way. The Terms of Service treat the skin, the alternative look of a character, and related items as Virtual Content licensed and tied to the account, and not as the consumer's property, and they state that virtual products may evolve over time, including for game balance, bug fixes or graphical improvements. There is a central tension in this mismatch, because the consumer knows the good through its aesthetic and community staging, while its stability remains subject to the platform's technical and contractual regime. That is why changes to visuals, animation, effects, symbolic balancing or access conditions cannot be treated only as functional corrections or graphical improvements, since they may affect the symbolic position that the platform itself produced. The contractual description is the norm the ecosystem declares for itself, and the legal qualification of what was acquired is a matter for the chapter on the object.

This media reconfiguration finds a counterpart in the ecosystem's own declared norm, insofar as the contract describes skins and related items as Virtual Content licensed, tied to the account, and not as the consumer's property.<1>p. 100</1>

The contract defines what is offered as “a license and a personal right [...] revocable” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. Then, it makes explicit the unilateral power to “delete, alter, [...] repackage, reprice” content, and states that “Virtual Products may [...] evolve over time”, including for “game balance, bug fixes, or graphical improvements” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>.<5>p. 100</5>

When the offer is structured as spectacle, but the object is legally presented as revocable or modifiable access, a tension arises that is central to the thesis: the consumer knows the good through its aesthetic and community staging, while its stability remains subject to the platform's technical and contractual regime. Therefore, changes to visuals, animation, effects, symbolic balancing or access conditions cannot be treated merely as functional corrections, bugs or graphical improvements.<1>p. 100</1>
The unilateral alteration of the item or the character may affect not only a technical utility, but the symbolic position that was produced by the platform itself.<1>p. 100</1>

From this comes the most important consequence for those who work with the duty to inform. The vulnerability of the digital consumer is not reduced to a lack of information correctable by more notices, terms of use or highlighted clauses. The duty of information remains relevant, but it operates within an ecology in which form, curation and visibility precede reading, since the technical-media presentation of the object has defined what seems visible, urgent, desirable or natural before any content is interpreted. Will is exercised within a repertoire of references and stimuli choreographed by the platform. It is in this asymmetry in the production of meaning that semiotic vulnerability is prepared, a structural disadvantage in the grammar of meanings that guides the subject's relationship with the object, treated in its own chapter, and it is also through it that architecture becomes practical normativity.

The offer comes to depend on technical curations, while the consumer's experience becomes continuously modulable. From this picture, the vulnerability of the digital consumer cannot be reduced to a lack of information correctable by more notices, terms of use or highlighted clauses. The duty of information remains relevant, but comes to operate within an ecology in which form, curation and visibility precede reading.<1>p. 103-104</1>

Before any content is actually interpreted, the technical-media presentation of the object has already defined what appears as visible, urgent, desirable or natural. Will is exercised within a repertoire of references and stimuli previously choreographed by the platform. It is in this asymmetry in the production of meaning that the category of semiotic vulnerability is prepared, understood as a structural disadvantage in the grammar of meanings that guides the subject's relationship with the immaterial object of consumption.<1>p. 104</1>
Architecture thus becomes practical normativity because it organizes the field of the perceived, the credible and the natural before the informational duty can produce its effects.<1>p. 104</1>
What loss escapes when one looks only at the altered attribute?

A rare cosmetic item or a character has value in the game because it functions as a legible social sign, a marker of identity and a point of belonging within a grammar that belongs to the platform. When an update alters the item's appearance, effects, perceived rarity or economic insertion, the compatibility between experience, narrative and recognition may come undone, and the promise of distinction remains in the account without finding, in the world of the game, the fit that gave value to the time, money and attention invested. Vanderburg allows us to read this frustration as the practical desymbolization of the acquired good, and not as a failure of technical performance.
In digital environments of continued enjoyment, the relevant loss is not reduced to the alteration of a digital object, but reaches the field of meaning that sustained its enjoyment.<1>p. 104</1>

A rare cosmetic item or a reconfigured character has value because it operates as a legible social sign, a marker of identity and a point of belonging within a proprietary grammar. When an update alters appearance, effects, perceived rarity or economic insertion, the compatibility between experience, narrative and recognition may come undone. The promise of distinction remains nominally in the account, but no longer finds, in the world of the game, the fit that conferred value on the investment of time, money and attention.<1>p. 104</1>
Vanderburg's usefulness lies precisely in allowing this frustration to be read not as an error of technical performance, but as the practical desymbolization of the acquired good.<1>p. 105</1>

Vanderburg defines desymbolization as the erosion of the cultural capacity to organize experience dialectically, maintaining relations of meaning that connect the elements of the world and give them compatibility. What matters in his work is the mechanism by which technique comes to operate from within everyday experience and filters what is lived, privileging what can be expressed in operational terms and pushing the rest to the periphery of what is perceived as real. The gain for the jurist is being able to describe the injury as the degradation of an enjoyment bundle whose core is semiotic and relational, and not as subjective frustration. And since the platform governs the repertoire of signs, the criteria of visibility and the routes of internal comparison, it also governs the conditions for verifying what was promised and what was delivered. What needs to be fixed, therefore, are the parameters capable of identifying, with minimal intersubjectivity, when a technical alteration relevantly downgrades an acquired immaterial good.
The consequence is that the conflict over system change ceases to be a dispute about taste or preference and becomes a dispute about controllability.<1>p. 106</1>

Vanderburg defines desymbolization as the erosion of the cultural capacity to organize human experience dialectically, that is, to maintain relations of meaning that connect elements of the world and give them compatibility <1>Vanderburg</1><2>(Vanderburg, 2011, p. 17)</2>.<3>p. 110</3>

Vanderburg, in turn, shows how this movement is incorporated into routines and translates into fragmentation and desymbolization of what is lived. Therefore, although there is direct continuity with the Ellulian matrix, the axis of the study in Vanderburg is the formulation of the mechanism by which technique comes to operate from within everyday experience.<1>p. 105</1>

When this mediation structures routine, it does not merely facilitate actions; it filters experience, privileging what can be expressed in operational terms and pushing the rest to the periphery of what is perceived as real.<1>p. 113</1>

This framing matters for the legal problem because it allows the injury to be described as the degradation of an enjoyment bundle whose core is semiotic and relational, and not as mere subjective frustration. When the platform governs the repertoire of signs, the criteria of visibility and the routes of internal comparison, it also governs the conditions of verifiability of what was promised and what was delivered.<1>p. 105-106</1>
It is a matter of defining which parameters allow us to identify, with minimal intersubjectivity, when a technical alteration relevantly downgrades an acquired immaterial good.<1>p. 106</1>

There is also an operational effect, symbolic captivity, a condition in which the repertoire of signs supplied and administered by the platform becomes the predominant grammar for interpreting the value, belonging and social world of the user, which reduces the routes of external comparison and the capacity to re-anchor meaning outside the ecosystem. The expression does not describe a psychological state of the consumer, but an architecture of mediation that selects, ranks and repeats signs through mechanisms of visibility, reward and obsolescence. In the observed ecosystem, the consumer has no way to take the good outside nor to re-anchor its meaning in an external market or grammar, and all that remains is to accept the new official interpretation of the object, because it is this interpretation that organizes reputation, belonging and social legibility. The player's frustration, therefore, is not collateral noise, but a symptom of a regime in which the platform administers at the same time the promise, the experience and the criteria for validating value.

This shift allows us to name a specific and useful operational effect, symbolic captivity. It is the condition in which the repertoire of signs supplied and administered by the platform comes to function as the predominant grammar for interpreting the value, the belonging and the very social world of the user, reducing the routes of external comparison and the capacity to re-anchor meaning outside the ecosystem. What is described here is not a psychological state of the consumer, but an architecture of mediation that selects, ranks and repeats signs, conferring on them practical centrality through mechanisms of visibility, reward and obsolescence.<1>p. 107</1>

The consumer has no way to “take the good outside” nor to re-anchor its meaning in an external market or grammar. All that remains is to accept the new official interpretation of the object, because it is this interpretation that organizes reputation, belonging and social legibility in the ecosystem. This helps explain why the player's frustration is not collateral noise, but a structural symptom of a consumption regime in which the platform administers, at the same time, the promise, the experience and the criteria for validating value.<1>p. 107</1>

The platform also manufactures ready-made frames of meaning and distributes them as consumable novelty. Riot treats skins as interpretations of alternative universes, which take the champion, the name the game gives to the character, to a new world under the question what if? The company describes events as packages of things to do, to discover, such as the lore, which are the stories released over the course of the event to deepen the universe, to earn and to buy. The symbol thus functions as a component of the device itself. On the contractual plane, access to content is described as a personal and limited right, and the supplier reserves the possibility of deleting, altering, removing, repackaging and repricing content at any time, so that meaning comes to be managed as a variable of the service, and not only as a marketing strategy.

Riot itself describes this functioning when it treats skins as interpretations of alternative universes, capable of moving the champion to “a new world” and reinscribing the experience under the question “what if?”<1>p. 111</1>

Riot describes events as packages that bring together things to do, things to discover such as lore, things to earn and things to buy, and it also gives Pulsefire as an example of an occasion in which stories are released over the course of the event to deepen the universe. The methodological value of such a formulation is evident, because it reveals that the symbol functions as a functional component of the device.<1>p. 112</1>

Access to content is described as a personal and limited right, while the supplier reserves the possibility of deleting, altering, removing, repackaging and repricing content at any time <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. In this architecture, the recycling of external symbols ceases to be merely a marketing strategy and comes to operate as a component of a supply regime in which meaning is managed as a variable of the service.<3>p. 112-113</3>
How do missions, passes and deadlines organize the player's time?

Technique incorporated into routines appears clearly in missions and passes, which organize the player's time as a sequence of tasks with their own inputs, outputs and accounting. The game remains, in appearance, a world of fantasy and competition, but it comes to be traversed by a second regime of orientation, quieter and more constant, in which what counts is meeting progress criteria, maintaining recurrence, not missing reward windows and converting time into currency in the most efficient way. The company itself describes objectives in which points are earned just by playing and sets the metric at 4 points per minute played, or 6 in case of victory.

A particularly effective way of denoting technique incorporated into routines, in the context of the empirical laboratory mobilized, is to observe how “missions” and “passes” come to organize the player's time as a sequence of tasks with their own inputs, outputs and accounting. The game remains, in appearance, a world of fantasy and competition, but everyday experience comes to be traversed by a second regime of orientation, quieter and more constant, in which what counts is not only playing, but meeting progress criteria, stabilizing recurrence, not missing reward windows and maximizing conversions between time and currency.<1>p. 114-115</1>

In official support, the framing appears in simple and operational language, stating that “some League of Legends objectives require you to earn points just by playing” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025f)</2>.<3>p. 115</3>

Riot is precise in defining that its missions credit the player specifically with 4 points per minute played, or 6 points per minute if they win the match <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2021b)</2>.<3>p. 115</3>

When the reward is structured as a track and the platform warns that certain items will be lost forever if not spent by the deadline, the horizon of the experience is cut into short cycles, and technique becomes agenda, calendar and criterion of everyday rationality, including in the form of prospective loss. The Terms of Service complete the picture, because the limited license to access virtual currency and content may be obtained by purchase or by earning, including by completing missions or game tasks. The contract states that what is unlocked is not the virtual product itself, but a limited and non-transferable license to access it. This arrangement is a temporal toll, in which access to content and currencies is organized by time invested, which becomes a route of acquisition foreseen in the institutional design of the service.

When the reward is structured as a “track” and the platform itself reinforces that certain resources expire, the horizon of the experience is cut into short cycles and manageable units, pushing the rest to the periphery of what, in practice, is perceived as important. In this kind of organization, technique is not merely a means, because it becomes agenda, calendar and criterion of everyday rationality, including in the form of prospective loss, when institutional communication warns that certain items “will be lost forever” if not spent by the deadline <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024b)</2>.<3>p. 115</3>

In the Terms of Service, Riot expressly states that the “limited license” to access virtual currency and content may be obtained not only by purchase, but also by earning, including by completing “missions or game tasks” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. The same contractual block also cuts off at the root any proprietary reading of “unlocking”, by stating that the consumer does not become the owner of the content, because “what you ‘unlock’ is not the virtual product itself, but a limited non-transferable license to access it” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>.<5>p. 116</5>

By turning progression into calculation, and reward into a regime of goals, the ecosystem produces an enjoyment that presents itself as fun but operates as a technically administered routine, in which access to content and currencies is organized as a temporal toll.<1>p. 116</1>

Skins and passes cease to be mere “extra content” and come to form part, as form, of the very regime of licensed access, in which time invested is converted into a route of acquisition foreseen in the institutional design of the service.<1>p. 116</1>

The argument does not depend on portraying the consumer as incapable. The reading does not suggest that they cannot distinguish game from work nor reduce the experience to addiction or weakness, because the point is structural and lies in the form. It is not a matter of moralizing the game, but of recognizing that this kind of environment educates attention and relevance through repetition. In the points metric too, the reading of a psychological intention of the platform is ruled out, and what operates is practical rationality, which keeps the analysis on the environment, and not on the disposition of whoever plays or whoever designed the game.

This reading does not depend on suggesting that the consumer is incapable of distinguishing game from work, nor on reducing the experience to “addiction” or “weakness”. The point is structural and lies in the form.<1>p. 116</1>

The point, here, is not to moralize the game, but to recognize that this kind of environment educates attention and relevance through repetition, and tends to bring experience closer to performance, reinforcing the symbolic impoverishment described by Vanderburg.<1>p. 119</1>

It is not a matter of the platform's psychological intention, but of a practical rationality, in which the routine of leisure is reconfigured as a calculation of efficiency between time and reward, instrumentalized as a structural incentive to stay.<1>p. 115</1>

The same diagnosis reaches advertising. For Vanderburg, advertising comes to operate less through information about the object and more through the manufacture of a symbolic shortcut that links the good to a lifestyle, and ads become poorer in informative content while growing more sophisticated in associative engineering. The mechanism itself points beyond the message, because, when desymbolization weakens internal orientation, steering ceases to depend on explicit persuasion and comes to operate by design, through interface choices, operating arrangements, interaction patterns and forms of governance that structure the experience before any message. The question of what the ad said remains necessary, but it does not exhaust the question of how the system positioned the consumer and made certain paths more probable than others.

Advertising tends to operate less through information about the object and more through the manufacture of a symbolic shortcut that connects the advertised good to a lifestyle and transfers to the purchase the promise of belonging, recognition and fulfillment. In this register, ads become poorer in informative content and more sophisticated in associative engineering, consolidating in the consumer's mind an equivalence between commodity and desirable symbol <1>Vanderburg</1><2>(Vanderburg, 2011, p. 204)</2>.<3>p. 118</3>

Taken together, the diagnosis shifts the focus from content to form. The decisive point is not only what advertising says, but how a technical-organizational system positions the subject within routines of stimulus, reward, visibility and comparison, making certain paths more probable and others almost impracticable.<1>p. 119-120</1>

When desymbolization weakens internal orientation and advertising functions as a prosthesis of belonging, steering ceases to depend on explicit persuasion and comes to operate by design, through interface choices, operating arrangements, interaction patterns and forms of governance that structure the experience even before any message. In Vanderburg, this process appears as cultural erosion and persuasive exploitation. However, the mechanism itself points to something beyond the message: a rationality inscribed in artifacts, systems and forms of circulation.<1>p. 120</1>
Why is a patch a decision, and not an accident of the object?

Feenberg comes in to prevent the environment described by Ellul, Postman and Vanderburg from being read as destiny, and with him technique comes to be examined as the institutional result of choices incorporated into artifacts, systems and governance routines. In games sold as a continuous service, known as games-as-a-service, patches (updates the platform publishes to alter the state of the service), reworks (broad redesigns of a character or a mechanic), changes to visual effects and adjustments to the internal economy do not function only as maintenance. They rewrite the conditions of permanence, equivalence and recognition in the ecosystem. Feenberg's reading allows us to ask about choices, purposes and responsibilities where the supplier tends to present only the natural evolution of the platform or the game.

In digital environments, especially in games-as-a-service, the relevant changes are not natural accidents of the object, but architectural decisions that redefine what it is, how much it is worth and how it can be enjoyed.<1>p. 120</1>

Ellul, Postman and Vanderburg allow us to understand the technical-media order as an ambience that reorganizes everyday life, and Feenberg prevents this ambience from being read as destiny. Technique comes to be examined as the institutional result of choices incorporated into artifacts, systems and governance routines.<1>p. 120</1>

The term “patch” is used in the technical sense of an update published by the platform that alters the operational state of the service (fixes, balance adjustments, changes to rules, content and parameters).<1>p. 121</1>

“Rework” describes a broad intervention of functional and structural redesign in a game element (character, system or mechanic), which goes beyond incremental adjustments (balance) and one-off updates.<1>p. 105</1>

Patches, reworks, changes to visual effects and adjustments to the internal economy do not function only as technical maintenance; they rewrite conditions of permanence, equivalence and recognition within the ecosystem. Feenberg's entry, at this point, allows this modulation to be treated as social rationality incorporated into the infrastructure, making it possible to ask about choices, purposes and responsibilities where the supplier tends to present only the “natural evolution” of the platform or the game.<1>p. 120</1>

What is presented to the consumer as a patch, balancing or conduct policy operates, in practice, as incorporated normativity, because it defines what is worth something, what appears, what gives status, what loses value and, through disciplinary mechanisms that may extend to banning, who remains authorized to participate. Feenberg allows us to treat this set as political rationality materialized in a system, which makes knowable the teleology inscribed in the interface, the rules and the architecture of sanction, instead of reducing the conflict to inevitable technical variation.
Platforms become legally relevant not only for what they “say” in terms of use, but for what they “do” in their architectures.<1>p. 124</1>

What is presented to the consumer as a patch, balancing or conduct policy operates, in practice, as incorporated normativity: it defines what is worth something, what appears, what gives status, what loses value and, through disciplinary mechanisms that may culminate in banning, who remains authorized to participate in the ecosystem. Feenberg matters here precisely because he allows this set to be treated as political rationality materialized in a system, making knowable the teleology inscribed in interface, rules and architecture of sanction, instead of reducing the conflict to mere inevitable technical variation.<1>p. 121</1>

Feenberg's most productive concept for the jurist is the technosystem, the integrated field of technically rational disciplines and operations associated with markets, administrations and technologies, which cease to be autonomous spheres that occasionally influence one another. Applied to digital consumption, it prevents the platform from being read as a mere technical performance. The platform operates at the same time as market, in its models of extraction and monetization, as administration, in private governance and in enforcement, which is the application and execution of rules by the platform itself, including through automated mechanisms, and as technology, in the architecture of mediation. The dogmatic consequence is that supply comes to be seen as an integrated sociotechnical arrangement, and the product of Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> cannot be isolated from the regime of visibility, accessibility and modulation that constitutes it. Immaterial consumption appears as governed enjoyment, and the consumer experiences at the same time content and the technical and organizational conditions of access to it, which operate by functioning criteria and are not exhausted by the traditional duty of information.

Instead of treating “technology”, “market” and “administration” as autonomous spheres that occasionally influence one another, the technosystem describes an integrated field of technically rational disciplines and operations associated with these three domains <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 16)</2>.<3>p. 124</3>

[...] digital, this prevents the platform from being read as a mere technical performance, because it operates simultaneously as market (models of extraction and monetization), as administration (private governance and enforcement) and as technology (architecture of mediation).<1>p. 125</1>
Usual corporate term for procedures of application and execution of rules by the platform, including through automated mechanisms.<1>p. 125</1>

The dogmatic relevance of this framing is clear. Supply ceases to be understood as a simple performance and comes to be seen as an integrated sociotechnical arrangement, in which what the consumer receives is inseparable from the way access, permanence, modulation and loss are administered by technically rational operations <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 16)</2>.<3>p. 125</3>

If the consumed experience depends on continuous mediations and if these mediations are entangled in markets and administrations, then the “product” (as defined under art. 3, §1 of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>) cannot be isolated from the regime of visibility, accessibility and modulation that constitutes it <3>Feenberg</3><4>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 16)</4>. Immaterial consumption appears, here, as governed enjoyment. The consumer simultaneously experiences content and the technical and organizational conditions of access to that content, conditions that operate by functioning criteria and are not exhausted by the traditional duty of information.<5>p. 125</5>
How does the rule move from the clause to the interface?

Feenberg sums up the premise by saying that no technology is an island, because every technology is mediated by markets and administrations. If so, design choices are socially situated decisions, open to criticism as to the purposes they fulfill and the asymmetries they produce, and therefore they are a site of attribution and of assessment of legitimacy.
The platform should not be naturalized as a simple medium, as if it were a neutral engineering unit to which the social would be added later.<1>p. 126</1>

From there, Feenberg formulates a highly productive premise for the legal critique of platforms: no technology is an island because every technology is mediated by markets and administrations.<1>p. 126</1>

If technology is always mediated by economic and administrative rationalities, then design choices must be read as socially situated decisions, open to criticism as to the purposes they fulfill and the asymmetries they produce, that is, as a locus of attribution and of assessment of legitimacy.<1>p. 126</1>

Non-neutrality has a concrete translation in the interface. Feenberg observes that arrangements of neutral appearance may incorporate unconscious preferences, and, in digital consumption, what becomes visible, recommendable, frictioned, permitted or rewarded may operate as interface naturalness and mask value choices under the idiom of functionality. Defaults, the options already checked in advance, along with hierarchies of choice, urgency devices and reward regimes, guide conduct without needing to declare the value orientation that informs them. Therefore, even without a lie or omission in the text, practical normativity can induce perceptions, desires and permanence through a grammar of interaction presented as simple usability.

Non-neutrality does not present itself only as an abstract thesis. Feenberg observes that technically apparent arrangements of neutrality may incorporate unconscious preferences. In digital consumption, this has an immediate consequence, because the practical normativity of platforms (what becomes visible, recommendable, frictioned, permitted or rewarded) may operate as interface “naturalness”, masking value choices under the idiom of functionality.<1>p. 128</1>

Default patterns, hierarchies of choice, urgency devices and reward regimes guide conduct without needing to declare the value orientation that informs them. Even without a textual lie or omission, practical normativity can induce perceptions, desires and permanence through a grammar of interaction presented as simple usability.<1>p. 128</1>

Feenberg also describes constraints materialized in systems capable of determining individual actions more effectively than political authority, because they bear on reflexes, skills and attitudes. When conduct is administered by systems and interfaces, governance ceases to operate only by explicit command and comes to operate by architecture, and the regime in which the consumer decides in the face of statements is distinguished from the one in which they decide within an environment that organizes microstructures of choice. In this second regime, legal responses cannot be restricted to clauses and notices. When constraints and incentives are integrated into the system to produce permanence, extraction and dependence under the appearance of enjoyment, the purpose ceases to appear as a side effect and comes to compose the material form of supply.

Feenberg formulates the normative dimension of design by describing constraints materialized in systems capable of determining individual actions more effectively than political authority, bearing on reflexes, skills and attitudes <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 36)</2>. When conduct is administered by systems and interfaces, governance ceases to operate only by explicit command and comes to operate by architecture. Platforms, in this sense, function as everyday governance, and legal responses cannot be restricted to clauses and notices when practical normativity is inscribed in the design <3>Feenberg</3><4>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 36-38)</4>.<5>p. 128-129</5>

The passage from explicit command to architecture as governance allows us to distinguish a regime in which the consumer decides in the face of statements from another in which they decide within an environment that organizes microstructures of choice. This shift makes the purpose incorporated into design legally relevant. When constraints and incentives are integrated into the system to produce permanence, extraction and dependence under the appearance of enjoyment, teleology ceases to appear as a side effect and comes to compose the material form of supply <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 36-38)</2>.<3>p. 129</3>

The last link is the design code. For Feenberg, the result of struggles and collaborations is the stabilized intersection between social choice and technical specification, and it follows that the consumed object includes the set of mediations that makes the content enjoyable, monetizable and governable, and that this code can be assessed as to the purpose it fulfills. Once stabilized, the code tends to reproduce itself through institutional inertia and through legal and economic mechanisms that make alternatives more expensive, and intellectual property appears as an infrastructure of semiotic and technical governance, which delimits uses, restricts reconfigurations and consolidates the supplier's authority over the conditions of enjoyment. When the technical code defines conditions of enjoyment, permanence and loss, the asymmetry between supplier and consumer ceases to be a mere informational defect and becomes architectural structure, a field of legal relevance that opens the way to the qualification of the teleology inscribed in the architecture, the subject of the chapter on abusive teleology and the unlawful act of architecture.

Feenberg asserts that the result of struggles and collaborations is a design code, that is, the stabilized intersection between social choice and technical specification <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 93)</2>. For the IOC regime, this is decisive because the consumed object is not reduced to the final content; it includes the set of mediations that makes this content enjoyable, monetizable and governable.<3>p. 129</3>

At the same time, the code can be critically assessed as to the purpose it fulfills, opening the way to the subsequent qualification of the teleology inscribed in architecture and governance.<1>p. 129-130</1>

Once stabilized, the code tends to reproduce itself through institutional inertia, path dependencies and legal and economic mechanisms that make alternatives and reappropriations more expensive. In this scenario, intellectual property appears as an infrastructure of semiotic and technical governance. It not only protects creations, but helps to delimit uses, restrict reconfigurations and consolidate the supplier's authority over the conditions of enjoyment, reinforcing the private character of the code that organizes the experience <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 93)</2>.<3>p. 130</3>

When the technical code defines conditions of enjoyment, permanence and loss, the asymmetry between supplier and consumer is not a mere informational defect, but architectural structure and, therefore, a field of legal relevance <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 101)</2>.<3>p. 136</3>
What place is left for law in the face of design?

So that the critique does not fall into a pessimism with no way out, Feenberg relies on a critical constructivism, according to which technology is neither value-neutral nor universal and, for that very reason, admits democratic interventions in the technosystem. He gives the name democratic rationalization to the interventions of users and subordinate actors that impose on technical development needs that had been ignored, or that run against hierarchies already stabilized in the technical form. He gives two examples, AIDS patients, who reoriented clinical research, and the users of the French Minitel, who introduced human communication into a network planned to distribute data. It follows from these examples that democratic intervention need not mean only external regulation and can be a dispute internal to the technical form and to the governance that administers it.

To prevent this critique from falling into a pessimistic substantivism, Feenberg anchors himself in a critical constructivism, according to which technology is neither value-neutral nor universal and, precisely for that reason, admits an explicit theory of democratic interventions in the technosystem <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 38)</2>.<3>p. 126</3>

“Democratic rationalization”, in Feenberg, is not a metaphor for “participation” in a generic sense. It is presented as a principle by which interventions of users and subordinate actors manage to impose on technical development needs that were ignored or to run against hierarchies already stabilized in the technical form.<1>p. 126</1>

Instead of participating individually as objects of a procedure, the activists act as an organized interested party and reorient the system toward new purposes, pressing for experimentation to become a standard form of care for the incurably ill and for the design of protocols to reflect, more responsively, the needs and urgencies of those who live with the condition.<1>p. 127</1>

The fact that the terminal “disguised itself” as a telephone device suggested to some users that the network could serve for interpersonal communication. From there, users “hacked” the network in which they were embedded and altered its functioning, introducing practices of online human communication, such as anonymous chat, aimed at fun, companionship and meetings, where mere data distribution had been planned.<1>p. 135</1>

First, the example shows that “democratic intervention” need not mean only external regulation; it can mean a dispute internal to the technical form and to the governance that administers it.<1>p. 127</1>

It is at this point that open auditability and functional value equivalence appear for the first time. If technique is constructed and disputed, these requirements can be read as parameters for the democratization of design, minimal material conditions so that the addressee is not reduced to a mere executor of an architectural script oriented by extraction and organizational predictability. This reading lets us understand legal criteria as ways of reorienting technical rationality without assuming that law stands purely outside it, and Feenberg describes the mechanism by which an ethical demand, once it becomes legally enforceable, stabilizes as a technical requirement and comes to form part of the system's regime of compliance and functioning. The two requirements appear here only as a horizon, and the construction of each is left to its own chapter.

If technique is constructed and disputed, requirements such as open auditability and functional value equivalence can be read, from now on, as parameters for the democratization of design. They do not function as rhetorical ornaments of transparency, but as minimal material conditions so that the addressee is not reduced to the position of a mere executor of an architectural script oriented by extraction and organizational predictability <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 36-38)</2>.<3>p. 126-127</3>

The idea of democratic interventions in the technosystem is of objective interest because it allows us to understand legal criteria as forms of reorienting technical rationality without presupposing a “pure” externality of law.<1>p. 127</1>
Feenberg describes a mechanism by which ethical demands can be stabilized as technical requirements when they become legally enforceable.<1>p. 126</1>
Once materialized, the requirement ceases to circulate as moral debate and comes to form part of the technical regime of compliance and functioning.<1>p. 126</1>

Feenberg also offers a reading of consent. In revisiting industrial labor, he shows how the union of capital and science can reduce the workers' task to the exercise of vigilance and dexterity. In formulating the notion of operational autonomy, he turns to Karl Marx to argue that the capitalist form of organizing labor gains technical reality when machinery turns the worker into a subordinate component of a preconstituted system. The example is not digital and matters for its structural function, that of showing that technical decisions can serve purposes of control and predictability. Transposed to consumption, the asymmetry appears as the supplier's operational autonomy, and the successful architecture is the one that reduces the operator's dependence on users, converts participation into data and value and does not generate an equivalent power to define purposes. Consent then tends to operate under low contestability, because the consumer adheres to a regime whose rationality has already been decided and incorporated into the system.

In revisiting the theme of industrial labor, Feenberg exposes how the union of capital and science can be oriented toward reducing the workers' task to the exercise of vigilance and dexterity, reorganizing dependencies and reinforcing management's decision-making autonomy. Although the example is not digital, its function here is structural. It shows that technical decisions can be oriented by purposes of control and predictability and that this control materializes in technical form.<1>p. 133</1>

In formulating the notion of “operational autonomy”, Feenberg <1>(2002, p. 43)</1> seeks to demonstrate that capitalist control of the production process is not exercised only by legal-formal command or administrative coordination, but is consolidated when the very organization of labor is technically incorporated. It is at this point that the author turns to Karl Marx (citing an edition of Capital published in 1906) to argue that the specifically capitalist form of organizing the labor process comes to acquire a palpable technical reality insofar as machinery and productive arrangements turn the worker into a subordinate component of a preconstituted material system.<2>p. 133-134</2>

When this logic is transposed to consumption, the typical asymmetry of the technosystem appears as the supplier's operational autonomy. A successful architecture is one that reduces the operator's dependence on the subjects who use it, converts participation into data and value and does not generate an equivalent power to define purposes. In this scenario, consent tends to operate under material conditions of low contestability, because the consumer adheres to an operating regime whose rationality has already been decided and incorporated into the system, which deepens the distance between formal choice and practical governance <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 54-55)</2>.<3>p. 133-134</3>
What does the balancing of the champion Mel show behind a technical adjustment?

The case that shows the political rationality of design is the balancing of League of Legends. The meta, short for metagame, is the set of dominant strategies and optimal choices stabilized in a given period, produced and corrected by buffs, which deliberately increase the power of a character, item or ability, and by nerfs, which reduce it. Buffs and nerfs are no mere accessory to the game. They are the means by which the ecosystem defines, in regular cycles, which characters and strategies remain viable and which fall, for a period, to suboptimal choices. The patch operates there as a norm in operation, because it reconfigures the competitive utility of assets, redistributes frequency of use and alters the real cost of staying. The update makes functional obsolescence an ordinary component of enjoyment, since what was learned, mastered and chosen can be downgraded within weeks by unilateral technical decision.

The term “meta” is used in the technical sense of the competitive gaming ecosystem, as short for metagame. It is the set of dominant strategies, optimal choices and performance patterns stabilized in a given time frame, resulting from the interaction between rules, updates and the aggregate behavior of the community.<1>p. 121</1>

The English word “buff” designates a deliberate increase in the power and effectiveness of a game element (character, item, ability, system), with measurable impact on performance and on the metagame.<1>p. 121</1>

In League of Legends, buffs and nerfs are not an ornament added to the game, but the very means by which the ecosystem defines, in regular cycles, which characters and strategies remain competitively viable and which are, for a period, downgraded to the condition of suboptimal choices. In this key, the patch operates as a norm in operation. It does not merely readjust variables, but reconfigures, in practice, the competitive utility of the enjoyed assets, redistributes frequency of use, repositions preferences and alters the real “cost” of remaining in the environment, since what is functionally strong tends to concentrate attention, learning and investment of time.<1>p. 121</1>

If the meta is, to a large extent, the set of incentivized choices, then the update is not merely maintenance. It is the mechanism that makes functional obsolescence an ordinary component of enjoyment, since what was learned, mastered and chosen as an axis of performance can be downgraded, within weeks, by unilateral technical decision.<1>p. 122</1>

The company's own documentation treats balancing as a formalized procedure. In the Champion Balance Framework, Riot describes the goal of making buff and nerf decisions consistent and easier to understand, with measurable parameters, audience segmentation, combined use of win rate and ban rate and thresholds that function as triggers for intervention. The company also maintains a public chronological index of Patch Notes, which allows the regularity of the patch to be reconstructed as the normal mode of operation of the service. This practice is one of the company's most praiseworthy and one of the most functional ways for platforms to meet the requirements of open auditability and functional equivalence. Even so, the rationality that presents itself as transparency and predictability fulfills a social function, because it converts statistical performance into practical orders about what should be played, what should be avoided and what loses competitive centrality.

In publicly explaining its Champion Balance Framework, Riot Games describes the goal of making buff and nerf decisions “consistent” and “easier to understand”, including through measurable parameters, audience segmentation and combined use of win rate and ban rate, as well as thresholds that function as triggers for intervention <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2019a)</2>. The result is a technical rationality that presents itself as transparency and predictability, but that also fulfills a social function, insofar as it converts statistical performance into practical orders about what should be played, what should be avoided and what loses competitive centrality.<3>p. 122</3>

Among the many practices consolidated by the company, the regular maintenance of the public index of patch notes is one of the most praiseworthy and was a mechanism by which the company adapted to the dialectical business model it had established with its community. The practice is, for most platforms, one of the most practical and functional ways of methodologically meeting the requirements of open auditability and maintenance of functional equivalence formulated in sections 5, 6 and 7 of this thesis.<1>p. 122</1>

The contractual basis completes the picture. The Terms of Service authorize altering, updating, suspending and applying nerfs to features and parts of the service, including virtual products, with automatic patches and with or without prior notice, and they allow altering the purchasing power of the game currency, for example by increasing the number of coins needed to buy skins. Balancing appears, in this picture, as a regular exercise of governance by design, and the ecosystem as an administered economy, in which value and access can be recalibrated by unilateral decision of the supplier.

The Terms of Service state that the supplier may alter, update, suspend and even “nerf” features and parts of the services, including virtual products, and they also provide for the application of background patches and automatic updates, with or without prior notice <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. Balancing presents itself, in this picture, as a regular exercise of governance by design: a mode of administering the ecosystem in which technical choices cyclically reorganize the field of the possible, modulate competitive utility and reorder incentives for remaining and acquiring.<3>p. 123</3>

In Section 5, dealing with the availability of virtual content, the text provides that “sometimes, we may change the purchasing power of Game Currency (for example, we may increase the number of Game Currency needed to buy Virtual Products, such as skins)” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. This reinforces the idea that the ecosystem is not merely a set of items, but an administered economy, in which value and access can be recalibrated by unilateral decision of the supplier.<3>p. 123</3>

The episode of the champion Mel shows this rationality coupled to the symbolic economy of the ecosystem, and, to read it, there is no need to attribute subjective intention to whoever decided. The series Arcane, distributed by Netflix and produced with Riot's participation, extends the cultural centrality of characters beyond the game, so that the technical decision to introduce or reposition a character bears on a figure whose meaning is produced by cultural and marketing strategies. Mel arrived in the game as a narrative milestone associated with Arcane, with a date set by the company for January 23, 2025, and the character was introduced first by the series and only afterward by the game.

The series Arcane, distributed by Netflix and produced with Riot's participation, extends the cultural centrality of characters and narratives, reaching audiences beyond the game and reinforcing the visibility of certain symbolic assets¹ <1>NETFLIX</1><2>(Netflix, 2024)</2>. From this perspective, the technical decision to introduce or reposition a character does not act on an abstract object, but on a figure whose meaning is continuously produced by cultural and marketing strategies.<3>p. 131</3>

The episode involving the champion Mel allows us to observe, more clearly, how the technical rationality of balancing can operate coupled to the symbolic economy of the ecosystem, without any need to attribute subjective intention to the decision-maker. The framing works as evidence that the technical decision to introduce a character comes with narrative and temporal marking, organizing collective expectation and attention in the ecosystem, as well as directly capitalizing, within the game, on the investment previously made in Arcane, since it is a character first introduced by the series and only afterward introduced to the game.<1>p. 132</1>

The sequence is enough to support the claim that design does not act only as technical optimization, but as social mediation that regulates centrality, acceptability and functional value, including when this regulation is synchronized with cycles of prestige and scarcity administered by the platform itself. By defining which forms of protection will be allowed and which interactions will be taken as too frustrating, design produces a policy incorporated into code, which governs the experience without presenting itself as an explicit legal norm, and balancing, although wrapped in the language of game health, operates as continuous administration of the environment. For those who litigate, the case has two merits. It shows a design choice behind what looks like a technical adjustment, and it shows that this choice leaves records dated by the company itself, sufficient to evidence the qualitative alteration of the mechanism, with the potential to affect the practical expectation of enjoyment and the functional stability of the acquired asset.

The case does not conclude that balancing is unlawful or that the company acted wrongly. Balancing is a regular exercise of governance, publishing the notes deserves praise and the analysis requires no subjective intention. What it establishes is that the change is a decision with criteria, dates and effects, and can therefore be reconstructed and criticized. The legally decisive question then becomes which purposes were built into the architecture and which conditions of auditability make that choice open to criticism. If the alteration downgrades the functional and symbolic value that motivated the purchase, the examination depends on reconstructing what changed, the subject of the chapter on open auditability, and on measuring what was preserved, the subject of the chapter on functional value equivalence.

For the argument under discussion, this rules out simplifications, because the point is not to assert that platforms are only capture, but to demonstrate that capture can be produced by specific reorientations of functions that also sustain sociability, expression and collective organization. It is in this ambivalence that it becomes legally decisive to ask which teleologies were incorporated into the architecture and which conditions of auditability can make that incorporation open to criticism.<1>p. 136</1>
What does the community dimension of platforms add?

Feenberg refuses to describe the internet as a neutral medium, because it is above all a technical system whose social meaning is inseparable from its technical character, and he describes the dispute around it as a clash between a consumption model and a community model. The distinction shows that the platform is contingent, stemming not from any internal necessity of technique but from conflicts between purposes. In interactive entertainment, community resources such as many-to-many communication, sociability and belonging can be integrated into market rationality as an infrastructure of extraction, and the community becomes part of the product's economic value and of its monetization architecture. Belonging, reputation and identity continuity are therefore technically organized components, not spontaneous externalities, which confirms that the materiality of the IOC is relational and semiotic.

It is precisely for this reason that, in dealing with the internet, Feenberg refuses to describe it as a neutral medium, since he insists that it is, above all, a technical system whose social meaning is inextricably intertwined with its technical character <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 99)</2>.<3>p. 134</3>

The dispute around the internet, in this reading, is organized by competing models that Feenberg calls the “consumption model” and the “community model”. This polarization is useful for the study of digital consumption because it shows the contingency of the platform, since it does not result from an internal necessity of technique, but from conflicts between purposes and rationalities.<1>p. 134</1>

The distinction between the consumption model and the community model is especially productive for interactive entertainment because it shows how community resources (many-to-many communication, sociability and belonging) can be integrated into market rationality as an infrastructure of extraction. In other words, the community appears not only as a “social effect” of the product, but as part of its economic value and of its monetization architecture. This is central to understanding the concept of the IOC, because it confirms that the materiality of the object is relational and semiotic. Belonging, reputation and identity continuity are technically organized components, and not spontaneous externalities <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 99-105)</2>.<3>p. 134-135</3>

The distinction also rules out the opposite simplification. Through the notion of concretization, Feenberg shows that a single technical structure can concentrate several purposes and serve both public life and market life, depending on the technical code that stabilizes it. He observes that social networks serve commerce by serving community, with targeted advertising based on data mining as a central source of revenue. Two consequences follow for the IOC regime. The materiality of the object is architectural and relational, and the consumer's vulnerability must be read as factual vulnerability with a structural dimension, in opaque ecosystems where the correspondence between expectation and delivery, or between promise and enjoyment, cannot be verified immediately.

The notion of concretization allows a more precise reading of the constitutive ambivalence of certain functionalities. Why is the environment a condition of possibility of the Immaterial Object of Consumption?

The combined reading of the four authors shows a single dynamic from different angles. Technical rationality tends to expand as a criterion of everyday life, media ecologies reformat what presents itself as reliable information and relevant knowledge, and technique incorporated into routines fragments experience and opens space for forms of symbolic steering that do without explicit persuasion. Feenberg prevents the diagnosis from turning into fatalism, because technical rationality is institutionalized in concrete choices, stabilized in design, and therefore remains open to criticism, dispute and control. The techno-media order, the name of this whole, describes less a cultural background than a mode of practical coordination.

Technical rationality tends to expand as an organizing criterion of everyday life; media ecologies reformat what presents itself as reliable information, acceptable debate and relevant knowledge; and technique incorporated into routines fragments experience, reducing the density of the production of meaning and opening space for forms of symbolic steering that do not depend on explicit persuasion. Feenberg completes this picture by preventing the diagnosis from degrading into fatalism: technical rationality is institutionalized in concrete choices, stabilized in design, and therefore remains open to criticism, dispute and control.<1>p. 137</1>
In this scenario, “techno-media order” describes less a cultural background than a mode of practical coordination.<1>p. 137</1>

Digital consumption then appears as insertion into continuous operational architectures. The consumer comes to inhabit an arrangement of access, curation, permissions, frictions and update cycles that exists while the system works and while they remain integrated into it, and the consumed object takes on a relational and architectural form, made up of mediations that organize enjoyment, permanence, loss, modification and degradation over time. The decision to consume is rarely formed only by rationally comparing performance, price and fitness, and defaults, choice hierarchies, recommendation systems, metrics and urgency devices produce a grammar in which certain conduct becomes easy, other conduct improbable, and many alternatives do not even appear as alternatives. The vulnerability that forms in this environment is not limited to a lack of information or to classic economic asymmetry, because it bears on the capacity to interpret, verify and contest the very field in which the choice takes place.
Even when there is no textual omission, steering can operate through curation and architecture, before reading and often outside it.<1>p. 138</1>

The experience becomes inseparable from the conditions of its production. The consumed object takes on a relational and architectural form, since it is constituted by mediations that organize enjoyment, permanence, loss, modification and degradation over time.<1>p. 138</1>

Therefore, the consumption decision is rarely formed only by rational comparison of performance, price and adequacy. It is also organized by regimes of attention, reputation and belonging, in which value is staged, reiterated and stabilized by presentation formats.<1>p. 138</1>

The vulnerability formed in this environment is not limited to a lack of information or to classic economic asymmetry. It bears on the capacity to interpret, verify and contest the very field in which the choice takes place. The decisive gap now opens between promise and the effective conditions of enjoyment, between sign and delivery, between the performance of belonging and the monetization infrastructure.<1>p. 138</1>

Positive law already points to this reading. Specific regulations on software and related services recognize duties of functional continuity and technical support linked to the economic exploitation of the object, which shows that dependence on maintenance, updates and governance over time is an attributable feature of supply, not an accident external to the consumer relationship. Governance, in turn, is distributed in layers. Contracts, private policies, technical standards and property regimes over signs and access appear as overlapping layers of a single governance, and intellectual property appears as a legal technology for controlling signs, delimiting uses and stabilizing expectations of enjoyment. What is permitted, encouraged or punished may be inscribed in interface, flow and metric, and not only in a clause.
Terms and notices remain relevant, but they cease to be the main place where power is exercised.<1>p. 139</1>

The characterization of digital consumption as mediated and continued enjoyment finds support in Brazilian positive law, which already recognizes, in specific regulations tied to software and related services, duties of functional continuity and technical support linked to the economic exploitation of the object.<1>p. 91</1>

On platforms, this semiotic governance is reinforced by contracts, private moderation policies and proprietary infrastructures for the circulation of content. In this layer, intellectual property rights appear not only as protection of creations, but as a legal technology for controlling signs, delimiting uses and stabilizing expectations of enjoyment.<1>p. 91</1>

Seen in this light, contracts, private policies, technical standards and property regimes over signs and access appear as overlapping layers of a single governance. The offer is simultaneously narrative and infrastructure: it mobilizes belonging and recognition while administering visibility, repetition and reward.<1>p. 139</1>
What is permitted, encouraged or punished may be inscribed in interface, flow and metric, not only in a clause.<1>p. 138-139</1>

The rest of the regime is built on this ground. The question is no longer only the content of the promise and now includes the way the promise becomes operative and the mediations that shape enjoyment without allowing the addressee to verify them fully. The purpose inscribed in design can be reconstructed as a structure of purpose, and requirements such as open auditability and functional value equivalence will come to operate as minimum parameters of legitimacy for exchanges mediated by systems. The techno-media environment is therefore not an external setting for the Immaterial Object of Consumption but its condition of possibility.
